tasks.title: T-FIXTURE-01 (P2, high) — The acceptance fixture's saved bytes are NOT reproducible: three sizes from one source, so the tracked asset drifts on every rebuild
tasks.description:
Problem
The generated acceptance fixture is tracked. Repeated writes can change its bytes.

Measured state
TestProject/Content/Tests/TurboMCPAcceptance.uasset is tracked. It is not ignored.

Conflict
Content/README.md says generated fixtures are not tracked. The Git state does not match that rule.

Cause
The runner saves the initial fixture bytes. It restores them at the end of a run. Direct fixture commands can still change the tracked asset.

Proposed fix
1. Remove only TurboMCPAcceptance.uasset from Git tracking.
2. Add its exact path to TestProject/.gitignore.
3. Do not use a wildcard. The directory contains hand-made test assets.
4. Do not add only an ignore rule. Ignore rules do not affect a tracked file.

Required checks
1. In a clean clone, run the normal test runner. Check that it creates the fixture before a dependent suite.
2. Run one mutating fixture suite. Check that git status --porcelain is empty.
3. Run direct fixture generation. Check that it creates no Git status entry.
4. Check a runner failure path and a forced editor-stop path.
5. Check that every fixture-dependent command regenerates the fixture or uses run-suites.ps1.

Do not change code until these checks have a plan.

tasks.title: T11 (P1, medium) — Function from text, with its signature
tasks.description:
*** SOURCE: `Feedbacks/TurboMCP_TaskList_2026-10-13.md:166-173`, group P1. SOURCE IDs: FT-15 (S4), FA-03 (S4), FT-06 (S3). *** *** CARDED FROM THE LIST, NEVER MEASURED ON THE TREE. ***

    DONE WHEN
        - *** function add accepts inputs, outputs and local variables OF ANY TYPE IN THE SHARED FIELD SYNTAX (`T22`),
          AND OPTIONALLY A BODY IN GRAPH TEXT (`T05`). ***
        - *** the function RESULT NODE IS CREATED AND WIRED. ***

    *** AND THE LIST ATTACHES ITS OWN MEASURED NOTE, WHICH IS THE REASON THIS CARD EXISTS: ***
        *** "in these sessions, THE ENGINE GRAPH WRITER COULD NOT CREATE A RETURN NODE. It also ADDED THE NEW BODY NEXT
        TO THE OLD ONE INSTEAD OF REPLACING IT. The TurboMCP tool must avoid both problems." ***
        *** TWO ENGINE BEHAVIOURS, BOTH OBSERVED, BOTH SILENT - AND THE SECOND IS THE DANGEROUS ONE: a body that is
        added beside the old one leaves TWO bodies where the caller asked for a replacement, and the tool reports
        success. `86cb04de` IS THE SAME SHAPE IN THE FIXTURE BUILDER: `SaneProbe` IS A VOID FUNCTION, SO IT HAS NO
        RESULT NODE, AND ITS OLD GUARD MADE "no result node" INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM "the link failed" (`86cb04de`,
        `BlueprintEditorUtils.cpp:2301`: only a function with out parameters gets a result node). ***

    *** SO "THE RESULT NODE IS CREATED AND WIRED" NEEDS AN ANSWER FOR THE VOID CASE, TAKEN BEFORE THE TOOL IS WRITTEN:
    a function with no outputs has NO result node BY ENGINE RULE, and a tool that insists on one will either fail on
    every void function or invent a node the engine would not have made. *** *** THE `T22` DEPENDENCY IS REAL AND THE
    LIST STATES IT: this card uses the SHARED FIELD SYNTAX, so it lands after that one. ***

tasks.title: T12 (P1, high) — Atomic multi-asset batch edit
tasks.description:
Architectural decision
    Add a dedicated Preview/Edit batch capability. Do not call existing Edit tools sequentially: each existing writer owns its own transaction, compile, and save, so composition would create multiple undo records and cannot guarantee rollback. The batch owns the only transaction and invokes reusable plan/apply primitives without nested transactions.

Public interface
    Add `PreviewTurboMCPBatchEdit` and `EditTurboMCPBatchEdit` with one `Operations` UTF-8 JSON string. Each operation has an ordered `kind` and the arguments required by that kind (for example `graphRepoint`, `graphSwapCall`, `functionAdd`, or an asset/table operation), plus a stable `id` supplied by the caller. The preview returns the complete ordered plan, affected asset/package set, compile/save phases, and every operation's predicted change.

Required design
    1. Parse and validate the complete operation list before opening a transaction. Reject duplicate IDs, unknown kinds, malformed arguments, and any operation whose plan refuses. Preview performs no writes.
    2. Apply all accepted operations under one `FScopedTransaction` spanning every touched package. Existing writer cores must expose transaction-free plan/apply primitives; wrappers must not call public Edit tools or create nested transactions.
    3. Defer compile and save until every operation has applied. Compile each affected Blueprint once; save each affected package once. Report the ordered compile/save set.
    4. On failure, identify the operation ID and kind, call `FTurboMCPRollback::EndAndUndoActiveTransaction`, and report every operation that had already applied and was rolled back. No partial success response.
    5. After apply, independently read back every operation's target state and compare it with the plan. A failed comparison rolls back and names the mismatch.
    6. The first line is `unchanged` for refusal/rollback and `changed` only after all operations, compiles, saves, and readback checks pass. The result names one undo, one compile phase, one save phase, and the exact rollback scope.

Verification
    First measure whether one transaction can capture modifications in two Blueprint packages and an asset package. Then add a focused four-step batch whose third operation refuses: assert independent reads show no first/second/fourth change, the response names the third operation, and the rollback list is exact. Add a successful multi-asset preview/edit case and assert one compile/save per affected asset.

Rationale
    A batch is a transaction coordinator, not another graph dialect. It must reuse the existing plan cores while moving transaction/compile/save ownership to one outer layer; otherwise the API would claim atomicity it cannot provide.

tasks.title: T13 (P1, medium) — Pin-level link dump
tasks.description:
*** SOURCE: `Feedbacks/TurboMCP_TaskList_2026-10-13.md:186-189`, group P1. SOURCE IDs: FT-07 (S3). *** *** CARDED FROM THE LIST, NEVER MEASURED ON THE TREE. ***

    DONE WHEN
        *** one read lists every node with its TITLE, KEY AND POSITION. Each link is printed as
        "node title . pin -> node title . pin". THE OUTPUT IS SAFE TO PLAN A REWIRE FROM. ***

    *** AND THE LAST CLAUSE IS THE SPECIFICATION, NOT A WISH: A DUMP THAT IS "SAFE TO PLAN A REWIRE FROM" MUST BE
    COMPLETE AND UNAMBIGUOUS - every node present, every link named on BOTH ends, and every pin identified well enough
    that a later write can FIND it again. ***
    *** THAT IS EXACTLY WHERE `T06` BIT: "plain call nodes on other widgets printed as 'no node type ID, cannot be
    written back'", AND THE READER LISTED GETTERS AS "not reachable" BECAUSE THEY FED NODES IT COULD NOT PRINT. A DUMP
    IS ONLY AS COMPLETE AS THE POOREST NODE IT CAN NAME. ***
    *** AND THE KEY IS THE PROJECT'S OWN SINGLE AUTHORITY, `TurboMCPNodeId` - WHOSE AUDIT CARD IS IN `backlog` AND
    RECORDS TWO FINDINGS THAT LAND HERE: a graph name containing a COLON ROUND-TRIPS TO A DIFFERENT NAME, and
    `FindNodesByKey` DOES NOT NORMALISE ITS KEY while two of its four callers pass it raw. A DUMP THAT PRINTS A KEY THE
    READER CANNOT RESOLVE IS NOT SAFE TO PLAN FROM. ***

tasks.title: T14 (P1, low) — Session change list
tasks.description:
*** SOURCE: `Feedbacks/TurboMCP_TaskList_2026-10-13.md:191-194`, group P1. SOURCE IDs: FT-14 (S4). *** *** CARDED FROM THE LIST, NEVER MEASURED ON THE TREE. ***

    DONE WHEN
        *** one read lists EVERY NODE, VARIABLE AND FUNCTION that TurboMCP created, unplugged or deleted IN THE CURRENT
        EDITOR SESSION, BY ASSET AND BY GRAPH. ***

    *** AND THE CARD CARRIES A DESIGN QUESTION THE LIST DOES NOT ANSWER, WHICH IS WHY IT IS WORTH MEASURING FIRST:
    NOTHING IN THE PLUGIN KEEPS A SESSION LEDGER TODAY. `TurboMCPCallLog` RECORDS CALLS, NOT CHANGES - it has the tool
    name and the arguments but it does not know WHICH NODES MOVED, and it is cleared when the editor exits. ***
    *** SO THE CHOICE IS BETWEEN TWO HONEST SHAPES: READ THE ASSETS AND DIFF THEM AGAINST A SNAPSHOT TAKEN AT MODULE
    STARTUP (which is measurable today and needs no new bookkeeping), OR HAVE EVERY WRITER APPEND TO A LEDGER (which is
    `T02`'S 68-CALL-SITE PROBLEM AGAIN, AND `T02` ALREADY MEASURED THAT PRICE AT 59 DISTINCT FIRST-STATEMENT SHAPES). ***
    *** THE SNAPSHOT SHAPE HAS A KNOWN LIMIT WORTH STATING UP FRONT: IT REPORTS WHAT IS DIFFERENT NOW, SO AN EDIT THAT
    WAS MADE AND THEN UNDONE IN THE SAME SESSION IS INVISIBLE TO IT - WHICH MAY OR MAY NOT BE WHAT "CHANGED" MEANS TO
    THE CALLER. THAT IS THE FIRST THING TO SETTLE. ***

tasks.title: T15 (P1, low) — Cleanup helpers
tasks.description:
*** SOURCE: `Feedbacks/TurboMCP_TaskList_2026-10-13.md:196-202`, group P1. SOURCE IDs: FT-10 (S3), FT-05 (S3), DD-03 (S1). *** *** CARDED FROM THE LIST, NEVER MEASURED ON THE TREE. ***

    DONE WHEN
        - *** "Remove debug prints" FINDS PRINT NODES BY TEXT, BRIDGES THE EXEC LINK AROUND EACH ONE, AND REMOVES EACH
          PRINT WITH ITS STRING INPUTS.***
        - *** an optional "park" mode MOVES UNPLUGGED NODES INTO ONE LABELLED COMMENT BOX.***
        - *** the DEFAULT IS DELETE: "Users who keep work clean want unplugged nodes removed." ***

    *** AND THE FIRST CLAUSE IS THE SAME BREAK-THEN-MAKE THAT `T08` AND `T10` CARRY, WITH A DESTRUCTION AT THE END OF
    IT: BRIDGING MEANS BREAKING THE ENTRY-TO-PRINT LINK AND THE PRINT-TO-NEXT LINK, THEN JOINING ENTRY TO NEXT. IF THE
    JOIN IS REFUSED THE CHAIN IS SEVERED AND THE PRINT IS STILL THERE - AND `TurboMCPGraphTidy.cpp:1306` IS THE
    RECORDED INSTANCE OF EXACTLY THAT. ***
    *** AND "REMOVES EACH PRINT WITH ITS STRING INPUTS" NEEDS A MEASUREMENT: A STRING INPUT CAN BE SHARED WITH A NODE
    THE CALLER DID NOT ASK TO TOUCH. A `PrintString`'S `InString` IS OFTEN ITS OWN LITERAL, BUT IT CAN BE A VARIABLE
    GETTER OR ANOTHER CALL'S OUTPUT - SO THE TOOL MUST COUNT WHAT IT REMOVED AND REFUSE A SHARED INPUT RATHER THAN
    DELETING A NODE SOMETHING ELSE STILL READS. ***
    *** AND "PARK" HAS THE SAME RISK IN THE OTHER DIRECTION: MOVING NODES IS A WRITE, AND A MOVED NODE THAT WAS NOT
    UNPLUGGED IS A CHANGE THE CALLER DID NOT ASK FOR. THE CARD'S OWN "MOVES UNPLUGGED NODES" IS THE CHECK. ***

tasks.title: T16 (P2, high) — Real node sizes for every layout tool
tasks.description:
Source
    `Feedbacks/TurboMCP_TaskList_2026-10-13.md:208-218`, group P2. Source IDs: X-01, LR-05 and KN-01 (S1), plus the capture design note (S1). This card came from the list. No one measured it on the tree.

The problem, in the list's words
    "every layout tool used a default square per node. The tools reported success on overlapping layouts."

done when
    1. Layout tools get real node sizes before they plan. One way is to draw the graph off screen.
    2. Without sizes, a layout edit refuses unless the caller forces it.
    3. Every layout report says at the top when the sizes are estimated.

Verify
    Run tidy on a graph that has never been opened. The result has 0 overlaps with real outlines.

The shape this card shares with T03 and T04
    This is a tool that reports a measurement it did not make. "0 overlaps" from a default square is true about the square and false about the graph. T04 has the same shape, where a compile verdict came from the compiler's log alone. T03 has it too, where a save verdict came from a return value. T04's fix is the pattern to copy: read the source that actually knows, and say which source answered.

The cheapest clause
    Clause 3 is the cheapest of the three, and it is the one that makes the other two honest. A report that says "sizes are estimated" cannot be mistaken for one taken from real outlines. `TurboMCPCallCostTools.cpp` already does this with "(%d row(s), each with its call count)". Its comment says why: "a count with no denominator cannot be told apart from a reader that looked at nothing."

tasks.title: T17 (P2, high) — Layout rules and score that match a person's layout
tasks.description:
Source
    `Feedbacks/TurboMCP_TaskList_2026-10-13.md:220-234`, group P2. Source IDs: FB-01 to FB-05 and TD-03 (S1), plus the reference layout rules (S1). This card came from the list. No one measured it on the tree.

done when
    1. The score order is: no overlap, then fewest crossings, then no backward wires, then wire length.
    2. The rules are:
       - Nodes in one exec chain share a row.
       - A branch or a loop body steps one row down.
       - A loop body continues right on the same row, and "Completed" steps one row down.
       - A getter sits left of its consumer, level with the pin it feeds, with a gap.
       - Getters for one consumer are stacked in pin order.
       - A pure chain moves as one group, below-left of its consumer, flowing left to right.
    3. The fixer does not refuse a space problem that it can solve.

Verify
    Lay out a 30-node function with a loop and 10 getters. The result has 0 overlaps, 0 crossings and straight exec rows.

Why the score is an order and not a sum
    A weighted total would let a large crossing count outweigh an overlap. An overlap is the one outcome that makes a graph unreadable, so the list puts it first.

The relation to T18
    The six rules are T18's siblings. T18 asks that the report and the fixer flag a getter by the same criterion. This card is the criterion for everything else. Two tools that disagree about one property is the shape that T06 and T07 also carry.

tasks.title: T18 (P2, high) — One getter rule for the report and the fixer
tasks.description:
Source
    `Feedbacks/TurboMCP_TaskList_2026-10-13.md:236-241`, group P2. Source IDs: LR-01 and LR-02 (S1, S2). This card came from the list. No one measured it on the tree.

done when
    1. A getter is flagged only when it overlaps a node, or sits right of the pin it feeds, or is too far from that pin vertically.
    2. After a fix, the report checks again. It lists each finding that was not cleared, with the reason.

Why clause 2 has the most evidence behind it
    `TurboMCPWidgetRetarget.cpp:355-384` re-counts from the Blueprint after the write and says "the removal did not take. Report this rather than trusting the count above". `TurboMCPDataTableRows.cpp:574-583` calls its read-back "a measurement of the result rather than a restatement of the request". `TurboMCPGraphKnots.cpp:1376-1405` prints "the rollback did not restore the graph". A fixer that does not re-read reports its own intention.

Why clause 1 must live in one place
    T17's six rules and this card's three are the same kind of property. The list split them into two cards because the getter rule is the one that drifted.

First measurement
    Find which of the two holds the rule today, the report or the fixer, and whether they agree. A screen for both sites is cheaper than reading either.

tasks.title: T19 (P2, high) — Tidy: no false cycle
tasks.description:
*** SOURCE: `Feedbacks/TurboMCP_TaskList_2026-10-13.md:243-250`, group P2. SOURCE IDs: TD-01, TD-02 (S1). *** *** CARDED FROM THE LIST, NEVER MEASURED ON THE TREE. ***

    DONE WHEN
        - *** A CYCLE MEANS A WIRE LOOP. A WRITE AND A READ OF THE SAME VARIABLE ARE NOT A LINK. ***
        - *** a refusal PRINTS THE FULL CYCLE AS A LIST OF NODE TITLES. ***

    VERIFY
        *** run tidy on a function that sets a variable and later reads it through a by-reference call. Tidy does not
        refuse. ***

    *** AND THE FIRST CLAUSE IS A DEFINITION, NOT AN OPTIMISATION, WHICH IS WHY THE CARD STATES IT AS ONE: a variable
    SET and a variable GET are TWO NODES with NO WIRE BETWEEN THEM. A cycle detector that walks a "variable" edge
    invents a loop the graph does not have, and the VERIFY IS CHOSEN TO CATCH EXACTLY THAT - a by-reference call is
    the case where a naive walker finds a path from the setter to the getter. ***
    *** AND THE SECOND IS `C-P2`/`C-P7`: A REFUSAL THAT NAMES A CYCLE WITHOUT PRINTING IT LEAVES THE CALLER UNABLE TO
    ACT. `TurboMCPNodeResolve.cpp:336-337` IS THE PATTERN TO COPY - "a missing graph is refused WITH EVERY GRAPH NAME
    LISTED, so the answer contains the correction" - AND ITS OWN COMMENT SAYS WHY: "saying which class it is PREVENTS A
    SECOND IDENTICAL ATTEMPT." ***

tasks.title: T20 (P2, high) — Capture shows what it framed
tasks.description:
*** SOURCE: `Feedbacks/TurboMCP_TaskList_2026-10-13.md:252-259`, group P2. SOURCE IDs: CP-01 to CP-04 (S1, S2). *** *** CARDED FROM THE LIST, NEVER MEASURED ON THE TREE. ***

    DONE WHEN
        - *** the whole-graph capture SHOWS EVERY NODE IT REPORTS AS FRAMED.***
        - *** a frame that is TOO SMALL IS REFUSED, WITH THE REASON.***
        - *** THE RESULT TEXT HAS NO CONTRADICTIONS.***
        - *** the image is returned, OR A PATH THE AGENT CAN OPEN DIRECTLY.***

    *** AND THE THIRD CLAUSE IS A PROPERTY NO SINGLE CHECK CAN PROVE, WHICH IS WHY IT IS WORTH CARDING SEPARATELY: A
    READER HAS TO COMPARE THE SENTENCES AGAINST EACH OTHER. THIS SESSION HAS FOUND THE SHAPE FOUR TIMES IN OTHER
    FILES - a caption naming one thing while the text names another (`TurboMCPCapture.cpp:906`, verified true), a
    count that is a sum of three buckets labelled as one (`TurboMCPGraphReplace.cpp:192`, fixed), and a
    "described by the text" figure that double-counted the reused nodes (`:222-224`, fixed). ***
    *** AND THE FOURTH CLAUSE IS ABOUT A DIFFERENT LAYER ENTIRELY: AN ANSWER THAT CONTAINS AN IMAGE IS NOT THE SAME AS
    ONE THAT CONTAINS A PATH, AND `LookTurboMCPToolset`'S OWN DOC SAYS IT "lists the live Slate windows a capture
    could frame" rather than capturing one. SO THE FIRST MEASUREMENT IS WHICH OF THE TWO THE TOOL ALREADY DOES. ***

tasks.title: T21 (P2, low) — Layout report counts
tasks.description:
*** SOURCE: `Feedbacks/TurboMCP_TaskList_2026-10-13.md:261-264`, group P2. SOURCE IDs: LR-03 (S1). *** *** CARDED FROM THE LIST, NEVER MEASURED ON THE TREE. ***

    DONE WHEN
        *** the count is printed as "N nodes + K knots", SO IT MATCHES THE OTHER TOOLS. ***

    *** AND THIS IS THE SMALLEST CARD IN THE LIST AND IT IS STILL A `C3` SITE: THE NUMBER IS RIGHT AND THE LABEL IS
    WHAT DIFFERS BETWEEN TOOLS. THE PROJECT HAS RUN THIS EXACT REPAIR BEFORE - `3e6d8357` ("the dependency count is
    THREE plugins / FOUR modules - five doc sites now say which they count") AND `30e0de9b` ("three rows quote code the
    fix deliberately changed") - AND BOTH CONCLUDED THE SAME THING: A COUNT IS ONLY CHECKABLE IF IT SAYS WHAT IT
    COUNTS. ***
    *** THE MEASUREMENT IS ONE GREP: every layout tool's count sentence, side by side, to see which spelling each uses.
    THAT IS CHEAPER THAN DECIDING WHICH ONE IS RIGHT. ***

tasks.title: T22 (P3, medium) — One field syntax for all field tools
tasks.description:
Source
    `Feedbacks/TurboMCP_TaskList_2026-10-13.md:270-277`, group P3. Source IDs: X-10 and SF-03 (S4), DT-01 (S3), SN-02 (S4). This card came from the list. No one measured it on the tree.

done when
    1. Struct new, struct fields, variables add, function signatures and table rows all accept "Name: Type option=value". They all use the same parser.
    2. The table tools accept display names first, then internal names. A refusal lists the display names.
    3. "float" maps to a double-precision real, and the result says so. "real" and "double" are accepted.
    4. Each help text has one example with options, including "force" for a removal.

Why clause 2 is spelled out
    A display name is what a person sees. An internal name is what the engine stores. This is the only place in the project where two names exist for one field. `C-P7` says that a refusal must lead to the next step, so a refusal has to name the spelling the caller typed.

Clause 3 is already partly measured
    `test-vars-add.py:30-32` uses `Speed: float default=250 category=Movement`, and the tool accepts it. `test-types` has a `kind` question on record. The first measurement is therefore a grep of every field parser, not a read of one.

tasks.title: T23 (P3, medium) — Table row preview and read-back
tasks.description:
*** SOURCE: `Feedbacks/TurboMCP_TaskList_2026-10-13.md:279-284`, group P3. SOURCE IDs: DT-02, DT-03 (S3). *** *** CARDED FROM THE LIST, NEVER MEASURED ON THE TREE. ***

    DONE WHEN
        - *** A REFUSED LINE IS NEVER LISTED AS A PLANNED CHANGE.***
        - *** the read-back SHOWS EVERY FIELD, OR SAYS THAT DEFAULT VALUES ARE LEFT OUT.***

    *** AND THE FIRST CLAUSE IS THE `P8` SHAPE IN ITS PUREST FORM: A PREVIEW THAT LISTS A LINE IT WILL REFUSE IS A
    PREVIEW THAT LIES, AND THE CALLER WHO APPROVED THE PLAN HAS APPROVED SOMETHING THAT WILL NOT HAPPEN. THIS SESSION
    MEASURED THE SAME DEFECT IN `test-struct` - a save that reported success while writing nothing - AND IN `T16`'s
    "0 overlaps" FROM A DEFAULT SQUARE. ***
    *** AND THE SECOND CLAUSE IS A CHOICE WITH TWO HONEST ANSWERS, AND THE CARD ALLOWS EITHER: SHOW EVERY FIELD, OR SAY
    THAT DEFAULTS ARE OMITTED. WHAT IT FORBIDS IS THE THIRD - OMITTING THEM SILENTLY, WHICH MAKES A READ-BACK THAT
    LOOKS SHORT INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM ONE THAT LOST DATA. `TurboMCPDataTableRows.cpp:574-583` ALREADY PRINTS "MISSING
    AFTER WRITE" for a row that did not survive, WHICH IS THE SAME ARGUMENT ONE LEVEL DOWN. ***

tasks.title: T24 (P3, medium) — Struct readers include break and make nodes
tasks.description:
*** SOURCE: `Feedbacks/TurboMCP_TaskList_2026-10-13.md:286-289`, group P3. SOURCE IDs: SF-02 (S4). *** *** CARDED FROM THE LIST, NEVER MEASURED ON THE TREE. ***

    DONE WHEN
        *** a BREAK or MAKE node that uses a struct COUNTS AS A READER OF EACH FIELD IT EXPOSES. THE "FORCE EQUALS
        READER COUNT" RULE THEN APPLIES TO FIELD REMOVALS. ***

    *** AND THE SECOND HALF IS WHY THE FIRST MATTERS: A FIELD-REMOVAL TOOL THAT UNDERCOUNTS READERS WILL REMOVE A FIELD
    SOMETHING STILL READS, AND THE COUNT IT PRINTS WILL AGREE WITH ITS OWN UNDERCOUNT. A `BreakStruct` NODE EXPOSES
    EVERY FIELD OF THE STRUCT WITH NO PER-FIELD PIN ACCESS IN THE REPORT, SO A READER SCAN THAT WALKS PINS WILL MISS
    ALL OF THEM AT ONCE - WHICH IS THE SHAPE OF THE DEFECT RATHER THAN A MISSING CASE. ***
    *** AND THIS IS `T05`'S LESSON ONE LAYER OVER: `T05` FOUND THAT THE TYPE FINDER AND THE SPAWNER SHARED ONE SOURCE,
    SO A SUBSET WAS IMPOSSIBLE BY CONSTRUCTION. HERE THE READER COUNT AND THE REMOVAL DECISION MUST SHARE ONE SOURCE
    FOR THE SAME REASON - AND THE LIST'S WORD "THEN" SAYS THE ORDER: FIX THE COUNT FIRST, BECAUSE THE RULE IS ONLY AS
    GOOD AS THE COUNT IT READS. ***

tasks.title: T25 (P3, low) — Data table create, with nested rows
tasks.description:
*** SOURCE: `Feedbacks/TurboMCP_TaskList_2026-10-13.md:291-296`, group P3. SOURCE IDs: FT-12 (S4). *** *** CARDED FROM THE LIST, NEVER MEASURED ON THE TREE. ***

    DONE WHEN
        - *** a TurboMCP tool CREATES A TABLE FROM A ROW STRUCT.***
        - *** rows can be written WITH DISPLAY FIELD NAMES, INCLUDING ARRAYS OF NESTED STRUCTS.***

    *** AND THE SECOND CLAUSE IS THE ONE WITH THE MEASURED PRECEDENT: `T22` REQUIRES DISPLAY NAMES FIRST AND INTERNAL
    NAMES SECOND FOR THE SAME TOOLS, SO THIS CARD IS THE DEEPEST CASE OF THAT RULE - A NESTED STRUCT ARRAY IS WHERE A
    NAME PATH HAS MORE THAN ONE SEGMENT, AND A PARSER THAT HANDLES `Field` BUT NOT `Field.Sub` WILL FAIL ON THE FIRST
    REAL TABLE. ***
    *** AND THE FIRST CLAUSE HAS A `C-P10` OBLIGATION THAT THE LIST DOES NOT SPELL OUT: A TOOL THAT CREATES AN ASSET
    CAN FAIL PART-WAY, AND THE PROJECT'S OWN RECORD IS THAT `UPackage::SavePackage` CAN REFUSE A RE-RUN WHEN THE
    PACKAGE IS NOT MARKED FULLY LOADED (`06f6868d`, `SavePackage2.cpp:239`). A CREATE TOOL MUST BE RE-RUNNABLE, WHICH
    MEANS THE SECOND RUN MUST EITHER REFUSE BY NAME OR TAKE THE SAME PATH AS THE FIRST. ***

tasks.title: T26 (P3, low) — Show the dependents of a struct change
tasks.description:
Source
    `Feedbacks/TurboMCP_TaskList_2026-10-13.md:298-301`, group P3. Source IDs: FT-08 (S3). This card came from the list. No one measured it on the tree.

done when
    1. After a struct edit, the result lists the assets that the change made unsaved or broke. It offers to compile them.

Why the card names both words
    "Broke" is the measurable half. "Unsaved" is the cheap half. The dirty set is a package flag, and a scan finds it. The broken set needs a compile.
    This session measured what a compile verdict can and cannot see. T04 found that a compile's `FCompilerResultsLog` carries only what the compiler reported. An ensure during the compile was invisible until the verdict also read the log capture (`7153502`). A dependent list built from the compiler's own log alone will miss exactly that class.

"Offers to compile them" is a sentence, not an action
    Compiling is a write. The project's rule is that a tool says what it did and what it did not do. An offer is therefore a sentence the tool prints, not something it does.

tasks.title: T27 (P4, medium) — One node ID format, readable by a person
tasks.description:
Source
    `Feedbacks/TurboMCP_TaskList_2026-10-13.md:307-312`, group P4. Source IDs: X-02 and X-03 (S1), DD-02 (S1). This card came from the list. No one measured it on the tree.

done when
    1. Every tool accepts the short key and the long ID.
    2. Every node reference in a result prints the key, the node title and the graph.

Clause 1 is already known to be half-false
    This session's audit of `TurboMCPNodeId.cpp` found it. That audit card is in `backlog`. `NormaliseKey` exists, and only 2 of its 4 callers use it. `TurboMCPCapture.cpp:675` and `TurboMCPNodeResolve.cpp:343` pass the raw parse result. `FindNodesByKey`'s key test is a prefix test, so a short key does not "match nothing" as its own comment fears. It matches every node whose GUID starts with those characters. The measurement is already taken, so the first action is to read that card, not to derive it again.

Why clause 2 makes clause 1 checkable
    A result that prints a bare key cannot be acted on by a reader who does not already know which graph it came from. That is T13's "safe to plan a rewire from", one layer down.

tasks.title: T-METHOD-01 (P3, medium) — Every count in every card must state the scope it was taken over — 161 is a floor, not a total
tasks.description:
Summary
    A count was published from an estimate and then measured. The mechanism named first was wrong; the conclusion is the same and the numbers are now real. The rule this card leaves behind: every count must state the scope it was taken over.

What was claimed, and why it was wrong
    The first version said 68 of 99 reports survived and 31 were lost, because the workflow caps each report at 3,500 characters and a truncated report can lose its lines from the tail. The cap is real — it was set by hand in the workflow script — but it is not what removed the reports. The spill file holds the workflow's return value, and the tool truncates that value to fit its output limit. The 3,500-character cap affected content, not count.

What was actually measured
    `src-batch1-raw.txt` has 12 `FILE:` markers and 10 `FINDINGS:` lines, with 2 reports cut mid-sentence. `src-batch2-raw.txt` has 28 and 27, with 1 cut mid-sentence. So 9 of the 68 saved reports are complete-but-short rather than truncated, and the real loss is the reports the spill never carried at all: 40 audited in batch 1 with 12 saved, 59 in batch 2 with 28 saved.
    The surviving numbers are larger than the card's own figure suggested: the 10 complete batch-1 reports declare 168 findings between them — not the ~50 lines that fitted the cap — and the 27 complete batch-2 reports declare 118, which matches.

The conclusion, now measured
    "161 C3 sites" is not the total of the saved reports either. It is the total of the lines that fitted. 161 is a floor.

The lesson
    It is sharper than the first version, because the same mistake was made again inside the correction: a mechanism was named from plausibility instead of from measurement. The plausibility was good — the cap was set by hand — and it was still not the cause.

tasks.title: T-AUDIT-10 (P5, low) — AUDITED BY HAND 10/49: TurboMCPWidgetTreeText.cpp — 688 lines, one comment omits the character its sibling calls decisive, and no round-trip defect
tasks.description:
Summary
    `TurboMCPWidgetTreeText.cpp`, 688 lines — the dialect's text parser and writer, and the only file in the set with no transactions, no writes and no counters. The code patterns that dominate the material and source-control writers cannot occur here. One finding, and one suspicion checked and discarded.

What was found
    The scanner's doc comment omits the one character its own sibling calls decisive. `:89` says a bare token runs "up to whitespace, a closing parenthesis or a comment", but the code at `:96-100` also stops on `(` and on `;`. The neighbouring `IsPlainName` — the function that decides what may be written bare — names the missing case as the decisive one: a space, a parenthesis, a quote, a semicolon or a line break "would end the token early or start a comment, so those are the ones that have to be quoted". One comment is therefore complete and its neighbour is not, and they describe the same rule from the two sides of one round trip. A reader who trusts `:89` and writes a value containing `(` produces text their own parser stops short on.
    Fix: one clause — "up to whitespace, an opening or closing parenthesis, or a comment".

A suspicion that was checked and discarded
    A round-trip defect looked likely: `WriteValue` at `:118-137` emits a value bare whenever `IsPlainName` allows it, and `TakeToken` stops on `(` — so a value containing `(` would be written bare and parse short. Reading `IsPlainName` settles it: it rejects `(`, `)`, `"`, `;` and every whitespace character, so such a value is quoted and the round trip holds. There is no defect there.

What is right (do not re-investigate)
    `:35-44` explains why a scanner rather than a token array, and the reason is diagnostic quality rather than speed: the faults worth naming are positional ("unclosed parenthesis at line 12", "expected a class after `:class`"), and a scanner can say where it stopped while a pre-tokenised array has to carry a position on every token to say the same thing. All 24 diagnostics name a line — every `OutReason`/`OutError` begins `line %d:` and says what was expected and what was found (`:175`, `:186`, `:203`, `:210`, `:220`, `:257`, `:271`, `:279`, `:289`, `:299`, `:346`, `:361`, `:372`, `:383`, `:395`, `:423`, `:559`, `:575`, `:584`, `:598`, `:648`). `:117-136` escapes `;` as well as `"`, because an unescaped semicolon inside a quoted value would still be read back as the start of a comment by a reader that applied the comment rule before the quoting rule; `:159-164` honours that escape. `:118-123` writes an empty value as `""` so an empty string survives the round trip. `:56-57` returns `'\0'` at the end rather than reading past it, so callers can compare without a bounds test. `:66-69` is the only place `Line` advances, so a line number cannot drift from the position. `:73-79` treats `\r` as whitespace as well as `\n`, which is what makes a CRLF input parse.

Note
    The two defect families that account for most findings in the material writers cannot occur in a pure text transform. A defect count per file is not a measure of quality: this may be the cleanest file in the set because the shape of the work removes the opportunities, not because its author was more careful.

tasks.title: T-AUDIT-12 (P1, medium) — AUDITED BY HAND 12/49: TurboMCPOverrideRemove.cpp — 182 lines, the count that caught its worst bug is not in the answer
tasks.description:
Summary
    `TurboMCPOverrideRemove.cpp`, 182 lines — the shortest file in the set, and good code. It names the measurement that once caught its own worst bug, then does not report that measurement.

What was found
    `:88-95` records what the first version did: it called `RemoveGraph` on the event's graph, and for an event override that graph holds every other event and the whole body of the Blueprint — so removing one override destroyed the other three and the graph with them, taking the overridden count from 4 to 1. It was caught only because the count after the removal was read back and compared with the count before.
    The delivered answer carries no count. `:111-124` reads `bStillImplemented` through the editor's own list and prints "the editor now reports it as implemented: %s"; `:141-153` does the same on the function-graph path. So the one measurement credited with catching the worst defect in this file's history is not in the answer. A regression of that shape today would be caught only by `bStillImplemented` going false, which is weaker: deleting the event graph also removes the override, so it cannot tell "the override went" from "the override and three others went".
    Fix: `UBlueprintEditorLibrary::ListEvents` and `ListFunctions` are already called at `:113` and `:142`, so the before/after count is two lines away. Print it the way `TurboMCPMaterialInstance.cpp:359-365` does — "looked at %d level(s) in the chain, each for: %s".

What is right (a lot for 182 lines)
    `:71-72` names both shapes before looking for either: an event override is a node in the ubergraph and a function override is a graph of its own, and both are looked for because a caller does not know which one they made. `:80` walks the node loop backwards, which is the only safe way to destroy from a container while iterating it. `:97-103` performs the same three steps the editor's own node deletion performs (`Modify`, `DestroyNode`, `MarkPackageDirty`). `:111` does the read-back through the editor's own list, so the answer is the engine's rather than the tool's own bookkeeping. `:125` and `:154` both say the change is in memory and not saved, and to call `E-SAVE`. `:159-161` lists the overridden names when nothing matched, so a caller corrects itself in one step. `:52` and `:67` both begin with `error:` and name what is wrong.

Note
    The file uses no `FScopedTransaction` at all — the undo step is the editor's own, through `Modify()` and `DestroyNode()` — and it has no unchecked cancel. The 28 found across the tree are confined to the three material writers.

tasks.title: T-AUDIT-14 (P1, medium) — AUDITED BY HAND 14/49: TurboMCPEnumAdd.cpp — 311 lines, Renamed restates the request while ShownAs beside it is measured
tasks.description:
Summary
    `TurboMCPEnumAdd.cpp` is 311 lines. One finding: a counter that restates the request and is printed as if it were a measurement — in a block that measures its neighbour honestly.

What was found
    `:224-231` adds the enumerators, `:248-254` builds `NewNames` from `InPlan.Values` (one entry per requested value), `:276` sets `int32 Renamed = NewNames.Num()`, and `:302` prints "names set: %d". But `:301` already printed "values: %d" from the same input — the same number twice, once as the request and once as the result. Nothing reads the enum back to see whether the names landed. The read-back was available and is named in this very file: `:247` cites `GetIndexByName`, which is exactly the call that would answer it.
    The contrast is eight lines up, in the same block: `:256-274` takes `SetEnums`' bool return and refuses in words when it is false, and `:279-290` counts `ShownAs` only from setters that returned true — a genuine measurement.

The engine header settles it: `EnumEditorUtils.h:60` declares it `static UNREALED_API void`, so there is no result to ignore and there was no finding. tasks.title: T-AUDIT-16 (P5, low) — AUDITED BY HAND 16/49: TurboMCPTokenEstimate — 48 correct lines and one false universal (one finding withdrawn after checking the spec)
tasks.description:
Summary
    `TurboMCPTokenEstimate`, 48 lines. One finding was withdrawn after checking the spec; the second survives and is stronger than when it was written. The withdrawal is recorded in full so nobody files it again.

Finding withdrawn — the parameter is documented where a caller looks
    The first version of this card said `TokenBudget` is documented eight times in the header and zero times in the only published document. Checking the published specification settles it: `Spec/03_TOOLS.md:29` ("large outputs take `TokenBudget` (0 means no limit)"), `:163`, `:205` ("token budget: when the output would pass the budget, step down the detail"), and `Spec/04_FORMATS.md:190-192` ("### Budget steps"). So the parameter is documented in the tool reference and in the format specification, and `TOOLS.md`'s silence is correct and deliberate: measured, every one of its rows is a name index — a tool, one sentence, a source line — and not a reference.
    How the mistake happened, because the shape recurs: the measurement was sound and the claim built on it was not. One document was measured, then a conclusion was drawn about the documentation as a whole without opening the file whose entire subject is the tools.

Finding confirmed
    The header claims "it is an estimate, and every tool description that mentions tokens says so". Measured: no tool description in `TurboMCPToolsets.h` contains the word "estimate" or the word "token" as prose. The header uses `TokenBudget` as a parameter name and explains the cap, which is a different statement from calling the figure an estimate, and `TOOLS.md` contains neither word. The claim is a universal — "every ... says so" — and it is false. It is the shape a reader trusts precisely because it is specific. The repair is either to add the word to the descriptions or to delete the sentence; the estimate itself is correct and its own name already says what it is.

What the file gets right
    The header explains why not "characters divided by four": outputs are S-expressions rather than prose, and most punctuation costs about a token per character, so the naive rule undercounts by half and a budget built on it would let through twice what it promised — a wrong rule, the direction and size of its error, and the consequence of using it. `:22` computes `Total += (RunLength + 3) / 4;` with the identity stated so the expression is not magic. `:15-16` names the double-close before the code performs it, which is the easiest part of this pattern to get wrong. `:37-39` counts whitespace as 0 and every other visible character as 1, naming the four whitespace characters these outputs actually contain. `:46` is the second `CloseRun()` the comment promised.

Tally
    One finding withdrawn, one confirmed — and the withdrawal is the more useful of the two, because it removes work that would have been done for nothing.

tasks.title: T-AUDIT-17 (P6, low) — AUDITED BY HAND 17/49: TurboMCPPureChecks.cpp — 132 lines, zero defects, and the structural reason why
tasks.description:
Summary
    `TurboMCPPureChecks.cpp`, 132 lines, zero defects found. It is the cleanest file in the set, and the reason is reproducible rather than a matter of care.

What the file does well
    1. `:20-29` — "the echo is folded; the measurement is not". `arguments` is free text a caller wrote, so it can contain line breaks that would cut the report's line shape. `FoldedToLines` folds only the echo; the string handed to `AssetFromArguments` is the caller's original string, so the answer this tool reports is the answer the real function gives. A display fix that provably does not touch the value under test, stated in one clause.
    2. `:39-50` — an optional empty string is written so it is visible rather than absent, because a line that ends after its separator is indistinguishable from a line that failed to print, and the project has recorded that confusion as its most expensive one. The repair is doubled: `(empty)` is printed as a word, and `:121`/`:128` print the length as a number, so a caller that does not trust the word does not have to.
    3. `:100-108` — the same rule applied to the one case the tool cannot reach: "no spelling is not one key". A report that printed only `toolset distinct keys | 0` would read as a normaliser that collapsed everything, which is the opposite of what an empty input says. So it prints two lines instead: that no toolset spelling was given, and that this is an absent measurement rather than one key or zero keys.
    4. `:114-118` — the asset extraction's length is printed too, because that pure function fails silently when it is wrong: an asset name that comes back empty makes the per-asset totals quietly short with no error anywhere. The answer and its length are both printed, and the length is a number.

Smaller points worth copying
    `:63-65` accepts commas and pipes as separators, because the project's list convention admits either and a caller who uses the other should not get a silent single spelling. `:76-78` trims the echo only — a display change that provably cannot change the answer. `:110-112` prints the count, so a caller reads a number rather than deciding whether a sentence sounds like agreement. `:56-57` states its own safety as a property: it reads no log, loads no asset and writes nothing, so it needs no fixture, cannot race another suite, and has nothing to restore.

Why it has no defects
    It writes nothing, so the rollback family cannot apply. It declares no counter, so the dead-counter family cannot apply. Every optional value has `(empty)` or `(none)`, so the missing-count family cannot apply. And every claim it makes about itself is about a pure function of its inputs, which cannot drift from the code that implements it.
    The pattern across seventeen files is now clear enough to state: the defects live where a file makes a claim about something it does not control — an engine call that returns a result, a transaction that may not roll back, a list it counted itself. This file controls everything it claims about.

Fix it the way the project already does elsewhere: `TurboMCPPureChecks.cpp:114-118` prints a value *and* its length, because an asset name that comes back empty makes the per-asset totals quietly short with no error anywhere.
    2. `PreviousAnalyticsProvider` is declared, reset, and never read anywhere in the repository. `git grep` returns exactly two lines: the declaration at `TurboMCPModule.h:62` and `Reset()` at `TurboMCPModule.cpp:130`. There is no third occurrence — it is never read, tested, moved or returned. `:135-137` says why it is dead: the provider restores the one it wrapped only when it is still the one installed, so the provider owns the restore and this member is what remains of a version where the module did. Delete the member and the `Reset()`; the unconditional `Uninstall()` above them is already safe by the provider's own idempotence, which `:135-142` states.

What is right in these two files (do not re-investigate)
    `TurboMCPSettings.cpp:9-10` gives the empty constructor a reason: the defaults are declared on the members, so it exists only to give the class a body the engine can construct from config. `:16-19` distinguishes the two accessors rather than aliasing them — `GetMutableDefault` is what `UDeveloperSettings` expects, the engine creates one instance and keeps it, so the panel's checkbox cannot drift from what `SaveConfig` writes. In the module: `:17-21` justifies the registry wait by the failure it prevents (registering in `StartupModule` would leave the class unregistered with no error, and the editor looks fine); `:23-25` offers the panel early so a developer sees the honest "missing" lines; `:30-35` is the focus guard, with four measured failures behind it — four attempts from outside the process each killed the editor, because the message loop treats an externally hidden or minimised main window as a shutdown condition, and the guard does nothing unless the run is unattended; `:67-80` removes the delegate before the toolsets and the guard last, because the guard needs Slate to unhook itself; `:113-120` lists the analytics attribute names with their source and notes they are BLAKE3 hashes with no arguments, which is why the plugin's own tools write their own full-detail lines as well; `:121-124` keeps the provider that was already installed and forwards every event, so installing this cannot lose an event; `:135-142` calls `Uninstall` unconditionally, arguing from idempotence rather than a guard — and the guard-free form is the one that cannot go stale.

tasks.title: T-AUDIT-20 (P6, low) — AUDITED BY HAND 20/49: TurboMCPTraps.cpp — 202 lines, zero defects, and four failure states kept distinct
tasks.description:
Summary
    `TurboMCPTraps.cpp`, 202 lines, zero defects found. One word in one comment is optimistic, and it is recorded as the small thing it is rather than inflated into a finding.

What the file does well
    It keeps four failure states apart that most code merges into one. `:27-32` keeps the parser separate from the loader, so a parse failure and a missing file are reported differently, because they need different fixes. `:41-45` reports "the file is not valid JSON". `:48-52` reports "the file has no 'tools' object". `:97-101` reports "the file parsed but recorded no tools". And `:152-156` reports "no traps file could be read. Tried: %s" with every path, plus the error that rejected any file that existed and did not parse (`:148`). Four distinct answers, each leading to a different action, and the answer names every path it looked at.
    `:144-146` warns about a file that exists but does not parse even when an earlier file already provided notes, because the author will otherwise never learn their file is being ignored — the failure that is easiest to hide is the one this file refuses to hide. `:174-176` parses into a temporary so a broken later file cannot erase notes that an earlier file provided. `:184-186` replaces a tool's entry outright and says why: merging would make it impossible to remove a trap that no longer applies, which is argued from what the user needs to be able to do rather than from what is convenient to implement. `:191-197` builds the table once in a function-local static, which is thread safe in C++11 and matters because tool calls can arrive on a worker thread. `:122-125` adds the engine copy only when it is not the same path as the shipped one, so a project carrying its own copy does not read the same file twice. `:110-118` builds every path through `FPaths::Combine`, so no absolute machine path appears anywhere in the file.

The one thing to change
    `:109` says "shipped notes first, so a project file can add to or correct them", but `LoadFile` replaces a tool's entry outright and the comment at `:184-186` explains why. A project file can therefore correct a shipped note and cannot add one to it. The comment at `:184` is right and the one at `:109` is more optimistic than the code. One clause to fix.

tasks.title: T-AUDIT-22 (P1, medium) — AUDITED BY HAND 22/49: TurboMCPCallCostTools.cpp read to the end — a substituted cap parameter, and reporting discipline the three material writers lack
tasks.description:
Summary
    `TurboMCPCallCostTools.cpp` (403 lines) was read to the end. The first finding held; the second was too strong and is narrowed here after reading the rest of the file. The same file is also the best reporting example in the whole audit.

What was found
    1. An unreadable numeric parameter is silently replaced — the second instance of this pattern in two files. In `TurboMCPTypes.cpp:395-404` and again at `TurboMCPCallCostTools.cpp:114-122`, a value that fails to parse falls back to the default: `banana`, `0` and `-5` all produce the answer for 50 (types) or 10 (this file). A refused value and an accepted value print the same line. Fix: refuse the bad value by name, the way `TurboMCPTypes.cpp:407` now does.
    2. Narrowed: the earlier note said `FMath::Min(Wanted, 50)` "bounds silently". That was too strong. The ceiling itself is not announced (`:123`), but every truncation it causes is: `:349` and `:382` print "... and %d more. RAISE CAP TO SEE THEM.", `:344` and `:377` put the row count in the heading, `:177` says how many log entries did not match the filter, and every row carries tokens, characters and milliseconds together. So the repair is one sentence — say the cap is bounded at 50 — which is what `TurboMCPTypes.cpp:351-355` already does with ", showing the first %d".

What this file gets right (the model to copy)
    `:87-93` states the three kinds of emptiness before computing any number, and the action each implies: logging is off means turn it on, on-but-empty means call something, nothing matched the filter means change the filter — reporting zeros for all three would tell an agent its tools are cheap when in fact nothing was recorded. `:100-104` says no cost can be reported and the reason is not that anything was cheap. `:19-32` records a defect found by running it: the qualified toolset was prepended to an already-qualified tool, printing `TurboMCPEditToolset.TurboMCP.TurboMCPEditToolset.EditTurboMCPCallLog | 1 call(s)`. `:35-44` records a second one in the same function: an unresolved hash written as "(engine tool ending 866fe74ba22c)" — human text with dots in it — so slicing at the last dot produced `866fe74ba22c)`. `:66-69` keeps two different problems apart: a call that returns a huge payload is not the same as a call that blocks the game thread. `:71-73` hands over structs the log itself parsed, so no second JSON reader can drift from the first. `:75-77` gives every total its denominator. `:111-113` bounds the answer rather than the analysis, so a total is never wrong because a list was short. `:125-127` counts every rejected entry. `:164-165` prints the log path and whether recording is on, on every answer.

Why this card is worth more than its findings
    The reporting discipline in this file — a count, its denominator, every truncated list naming what to do about it, every empty case naming the action it implies — is exactly what the three material writers lack. `TurboMCPMaterialTidy.cpp` computes `MovedBefore` and never prints it; this file prints "(%d row(s), each with its call count)". The cheapest repair in this audit is to move that discipline to the three writers, using this file as the model.

tasks.title: T-AUDIT-27-29 (P6, low) — AUDITED BY HAND 27-29/49: TurboMCPPlayCheck (.cpp + .h + Tools) — 757 lines, zero defects, and the correct form of what TraceTools does wrong
tasks.description:
Summary
    `TurboMCPPlayCheck` — the .cpp (570 lines), the .h (124) and the tools file (63), 757 lines in all. Zero defects found, and this set settles the `TraceTools.cpp` finding by contrast: it does the same job and does it correctly.

The refusal-prefix path is right here
    All thirteen `Answer.Reason` assignments in `PlayCheck.cpp` (`:351`, `:370`, `:377`, `:390`, `:407`, `:428`, `:445`, `:456`, `:468`, `:477`, `:489`, `:513`, `:562`) are plain sentences with no prefix. The wrapper adds the prefix once, in a switch over the outcome (`PlayCheckTools.cpp:26-50`): refused gives "error: R-PLAY-CHECK was refused. %s", already running gives "already playing: %s", pending gives "pending: %s". Each outcome gets its own form of words, added in one place, by the layer that knows which outcome it has. `:41-43` explains why `pending:` is an answer rather than an error: the session is running and the caller is being told to ask again, which is the only honest thing a single call can say.
    That is what makes `TurboMCPTraceTools.cpp:39` a defect rather than a convention — it wraps an error string with `"error: %s"` without testing it, which is the one shape that can produce `error: error: ...`.

Two more things it does right
    `PlayCheckTools.cpp:20-25` says both parameters are strings because the engine's tool registry marks an `FString` parameter required whatever its default, so "not given" is expressed by an empty string rather than by omitting the argument — a limitation named, traced to the note `R-TOOL-SCHEMA` already carries, and worked around in the signature. `PlayCheck.h:27` states that `UEditorEngine::RequestPlaySession` starts nothing but stores the request, which is the distinction that makes `pending` a real outcome.

All four counters are read
    `PlayCheck.cpp:152-155` sets `WarningCount`, `ErrorCount`, `DroppedCount` and `OwnerThreadId`, and all four appear in the answer. `DroppedCount` matters most: a play check that dropped log lines has to say so, or a clean report of "0 error(s)" cannot be told from a report over a log that lost its errors. This is the third file in the audit that carries its own denominator without being told to.

Tally
    After twenty-nine files: fourteen with no defect found, fifteen with one to three, and the defects are concentrated in the three material writers and in refusal/convention divergences across files written in many rounds. No file that only reads has shown a defect that changes behaviour.

tasks.title: T-SUITE-02 (P3, low) — The FAILS ON convention measures a vocabulary, not a quality — two full suites tested, and one of the 34 silent ones is exemplary
tasks.description:
Summary
    This card's finding was tested against two full suites, and the test changed what it claims.

What was measured
    `Tools/checks/check-fails-on.py` reads 52 suites and 1546 `check()` calls: 18 name a failing input by the broad pattern, 9 by the narrow one, and 34 do not.
    `test-uncovered-tools.py` (176 lines) is one of the nine, and it also records the two wrong versions of its own checks — its best line is the best statement of the comment-versus-code problem in this audit: "the output is asserted, not the doc comment … a check written from a doc comment tests the comment."
    `test-asset-cost.py` (175 lines) is one of the 34 and it is complete. It has no `FAILS ON` line, and 14 active checks that each name what they prove: "it names soft references as their own kind", "the split states how many dependency entries were examined", "an unknown size comes with a reason rather than alone", "it says explicitly that this is not zero", "the refusal does not claim a zero size, which would read as free".

The conclusion, and why the first version of this card was wrong
    The convention measures a vocabulary, not a quality. A suite can satisfy every rule the template states and never write `FAILS ON`; a suite can write it and assert something its own author later recorded as wrong. That is exactly why the first version of this card was wrong to imply that 43 suites were defective, and why the tool now carries its own limit in its output.

The decision, with both costs measured
    Drop it: the phrase measures a comment, not a check, and `test-asset-cost.py` is the evidence — fourteen checks that state their own failure conditions without using the phrase. Removing the rule from `make-tools-doc.py` costs nothing that anything else depends on.
    Or rewrite it: "name an input that makes the check fail" is a good requirement, and `FAILS ON` is only one way of meeting it. As it stands the template asks for a sentence shape, and a sentence shape is not a property of a test.
    Recommendation: drop it, or rewrite the rule to ask for what it means. A rule that a good suite violates is a rule that will be ignored.

Keep the tool
    The measurement is still useful: 34 suites do not say what makes them fail, and a reader who wants to spot-check them now has the list instead of the whole directory.

tasks.title: T-AUDIT-31 (P6, low) — AUDITED BY HAND 31/49: TurboMCPOverrides.cpp — 402 lines, zero defects, and the fifteenth read-only file with no behaviour defect
tasks.description:
Summary
    `TurboMCPOverrides.cpp`, 402 lines, a pure reader — zero write sites and zero defects found. It is the fifteenth read-only file with no behaviour defect.

The measurement first
    No `Modify()`, no `MarkPackageDirty`, no `Transaction`, no `NewObject`, no `DestroyNode`, no `SetValue` and no `RemoveOverride` anywhere in the file. Its counters — `Shown` (twice), `Mode`, `Overridden`, `Matched` — are all read, and `:190` documents the encoding of the one that could be ambiguous: `int32 Mode = 0;   // 0 = all, 1 = overridden, 2 = available`.

What remains is the refusal and the empty case, both done properly
    `:181-183` refuses an empty asset and gives the form to pass. `:191` treats an empty filter as all. `:206-207` refuses an unknown filter with the accepted list and the escape: "error: '%s' is not an include filter. Accepted: all, overridden, available. Leave it empty for all." `:212` reports a resolve failure rather than absorbing it. `:222` refuses a non-Blueprint with the consequence rather than the diagnosis: "error: %s is not a Blueprint, so it has no parent chain to read". `:294` prints `(none)` for a missing parent rather than an empty field. `:298` prints "interfaces: none implemented directly". `:357` prints "from: unknown, no class in the chain declares this name", so an absence carries its cause. And `:136-137` states that a name with no reflected function is not a failure, because an interface member can be declared without a `Function` entry — saying so beats an empty pair.

The pattern, now measurable across the whole audit
    Fifteen read-only files, and not one has shown a defect that changes behaviour. Every behaviour defect found — the 28 unchecked cancels, the dead counters, the early exits that skip `MarkPackageDirty`, the substituted numeric parameters — is in a file that writes.
    That is actionable for prioritising the remaining files: writers come first, and there are few of them left. Readers can be checked for comment and refusal defects later, or by a check rather than by hand, because neither pattern changes what the tool does — it changes what the tool says.

tasks.title: T-AUDIT-32 (P5, low) — AUDITED BY HAND 32/49: TurboMCPNodeType.cpp — 1058 lines, and a note with a written contract that fourteen assignments fill and no caller reads
tasks.description:
Summary
    `TurboMCPNodeType.cpp`, 1058 lines — the largest reader in the tree. One finding, and it is the fifth instance of the pattern this audit keeps finding: a correct idea that is not wired to the place that needs it.

What was found
    An `FString& OutNote` carries a written contract, is filled fourteen times, and is read by nobody. `TurboMCPNodeType.h:140` documents it: "@param OutNote why it could not be built, when it could not. Never empty on failure." `:180` repeats the contract for `SpawnNodeOfType` with one stated exception ("never empty unless Spawned"). The implementation assigns it fourteen times — `:274` "no Blueprint", `:279` "no graph", `:337` "a transient graph for the probe could not be created", plus `:349`, `:358`, `:380`, `:385`, `:440`, `:461`, `:468`, and two `OutNote.Empty()` calls at `:270` and `:376`. A `git grep` for `OutNote` finds only two files in the whole repository: the .cpp with its 14 uses and the .h with 4 (the two declarations and their documentation). No caller passes it and no line reads it — a contract with no counterparty. The implementation does the work the doc promises; the string is discarded.
    The file itself shows where the note belongs: `:469-470` builds the refusal from `ESpawnResult` alone, so the caller is told *that* the spawn failed and never *why*.
    Fix: append the note where the failure is turned into an answer. One line, and the doc already describes what it should say.

Second item, recorded so it is not re-reported
    The transient probe graph. `:334` creates a `UEdGraph` with `RF_Transient`, which invites the "does a read change something?" question, and `:328-333` answers it with the reason: its outer is the Blueprint so a node that walks its outer chain finds one, it is not added to the Blueprint's graph lists, and so nothing in the asset is touched. `:335-338` tests it for null; `:135-137` states the caller's obligation, that the real graph's node count does not change and the caller owns the result. There is no `Modify()`, no `Transaction` and no `MarkPackageDirty` anywhere in the file, so it cannot leave the asset dirty.

Note
    That makes five instances of one pattern at five scales: a `kind` that `KnownKinds` does not accept (`TurboMCPTypes.cpp`), `NormaliseKey` used by two of its four callers (`TurboMCPNodeId.cpp`), a `mutable` documented in `TurboMCPPanelToolRunner.h` that the code replaced with a `const_cast`, a template rule that only 9 of 52 suites follow (`Tools/make-tools-doc.py`), and this one. The defect is the same every time and so is the repair: wire it, or delete it. What must not remain is a contract, a guard, a field or a rule that exists in one place and is consulted in none.

tasks.title: T-X4-01 (P4, low) — The X4 screen over all of Tools/: zero orphaned symbols, so the pattern lives entirely in Source/ where there are five
tasks.description:
Summary
    A symbol-level screen over everything in `Tools/`, looking for anything declared and never consulted. It found nothing there — and the negative result is worth keeping, because it says where the pattern actually lives.

What was screened
    With `Select-String` over every file, not `git grep`, which returned false zeros four times in that session.
    `Tools/checks/` (8 scripts): every function is called. `Report` in `check-plugin.py` is instantiated at `:453`, passed to all six check functions, and its `failures` and `passes` are read and printed at `:463` and `:467`.
    Infrastructure (3 modules): `tmcp.py` 7 functions, `tmcp_paths.py` 3, `tmcp_editor.py` 4 — and `tmcp_editor.rebuild_fixture` is called from `test-graph-replace.py:88`, `test-graph-structure.py:129` and four suites that wrap it.
    Generators (`make-*.py`, 7 files): 17 functions, none unused. Scripts (`*.ps1`, 11 files): 17 functions, none unused — `run-suites.ps1` calls `Invoke-SuiteProcess` at `:260` and `:345`, `Start-EditorAndWait` at `:309`, `Stop-Editor` at `:390` and `:402`.

So the pattern lives entirely in `Source/`, where there are five
    `TurboMCPTypes.cpp:116-119` — `KindOfType` returns "function" and `KnownKinds` at `:199` does not accept it. `TurboMCPNodeId.cpp:178-208` — `NormaliseKey` exists and two of its four callers use it. `TurboMCPPanelToolRunner.h` — the header documents a `mutable` and the code uses a `const_cast`. `TurboMCPNodeType.h:140` — `OutNote`, "never empty on failure", assigned fourteen times and read by no line. `Tools/make-tools-doc.py` — the template requires a phrase that only 9 of 52 suites use; that is the one `Tools/` instance and it is a convention rather than a symbol.

The contrast is the useful part
    The C++ side declares five things it does not consume. The script side follows its own rules when a gate enforces them, and not when they are only written in a template. `audit-suite-quality.py` blocks on six code properties and reports 0 candidates; the comment convention is unmeasured, and 43 of 52 suites do not use it.

What this card does not claim
    That the `Tools/` scripts are correct. This was a symbol-level screen — it answers "is anything declared and never consulted" and nothing else. The 43 suites have not been read, and neither have `common.ps1`, `build.ps1`, `setup-engine.ps1` or `start-editor.ps1`.

tasks.title: T-AUDIT-UNCOVERED (P3, low) — AUDITED: test-uncovered-tools.py — 176 lines, the best statement of C3 in the audit, and one weak check named
tasks.description:
Summary
    One of the nine suites that names its failure input, and the one that closes the coverage gap. 176 lines, and it contains the best statement of the comment-versus-code problem this audit has read.

Two lessons it records about its own first versions
    1. `:54-61` — the first version asserted the wrong thing and went red on two tools that were right, because it assumed a tool named `<Toolset>Toolset` describes its toolset. Measured, neither does: `LookTurboMCPToolset` lists the live Slate windows a capture could frame, and `PreviewTurboMCPToolset` measures this plugin's help output against the 2000-character budget. So the checks assert what each tool says it does in its own doc comment, which is the only contract it has. A check must assert what the call promises, not what its name suggests.
    2. `:69-73` — assert the output, not the doc comment, because the first version of that check demanded the sentence "it does not capture an image yet" from the header, while `L-CAPTURE` arrived in phase 3 and the caption now reads "look: editing windows, N visible". The header comment is stale and the code is right. A check written from a doc comment tests the comment — and that is the best statement of the underlying problem in this whole audit: the doc and the code diverge, and a test written from the doc validates the doc.

What the suite is for
    `Tools/audit-tool-coverage.py` reads the tool declarations out of the header and the calls out of every suite, and reports the tools that no suite calls. Its first honest run found five, named with their signatures: `EditTurboMCPCompile`, `LookTurboMCPToolset`, `PreviewTurboMCPToolset`, `ReadTurboMCPEditQueue`, `ReadTurboMCPNodeResolve`. A tool that registers and answers nothing when called looks finished in `R-TOOL-INDEX` and in the panel's tool list, and nothing contradicts it — a panel lets a human try a tool, and notices nothing about a tool nobody tried. `:21-27` lists what each check proves before the checks, including that every tool answers rather than returning an empty string, so a reader can see what is and is not covered.

One weak check, named because the card should be honest about the suite it praises
    `:74-75` asserts `look.count("\n") >= 1`, which is true for any multi-line output, including an error message that spans lines. It is not in the cannot-fail class — a single-line answer would fail it — but it is weak, and the suite's own standard says what it needs: a `FAILS ON` line naming the input, for example "fails on: the listing collapsing to one line". The suite names its failures elsewhere, so this is an omission rather than a habit.

Note
    `check-fails-on.py` reports that 34 of 52 suites do not state their failing input. This one does, and it also records the two wrong versions of its own checks — the standard here is high where it is applied.

tasks.title: T-AUDIT-36 (P5, low) — AUDITED BY HAND 36/49: TurboMCPGraphLoad.cpp — the spec and code are both honest about format 'write'; the plan's count is the only thing that omits it
tasks.description:
Summary
    `TurboMCPGraphLoad.cpp`, 170 lines, a pure reader. The first version of this card called it "a capability the spec promises and the code refuses". Checking the spec showed the spec is honest, so the finding is narrower and exact.

What the spec actually says
    `Spec/04_FORMATS.md:118-120`, repeated at `Spec/03_TOOLS.md:221`: format `write` prints a graph in the form the engine's own graph write tool accepts, because agents will keep using that tool until the plugin's writer is done. So the spec says the writer is not finished, and the code's refusal is correct and honest — `:97-103` names the spec section, says it is the next step of phase 2, and offers the fallback: use format `read`, the default, to read the graph now. There is no gap between the spec and the code.

What remains, and it is one thing
    The plan's count does not include it. `Tools/checks/count-plan.py` reads `30 todo, 16 done, 2 open` of 48 rows, and the graph write dialect is not among the two open rows; no `PLAN.md` row names it either, and no suite calls `write`, so the refusal is never exercised. A known-incomplete capability is therefore missing from the count, and the number a reader checks first reads as more complete than the project is.
    Fix: add the graph write dialect to `Spec/WORKING_PLAN.md` as an open item, or say in the plan why it is not one. Then `count-plan.py` counts it and the number is true.

How the first version got it wrong
    One file was read and a claim was made about a second without opening it. The measurement was right and the claim built on it was wrong — the same shape as the withdrawn finding on `TurboMCPTokenEstimate`.

What the file gets right
    No `Modify()`, no `Transaction`, no `MarkPackageDirty`. Every refusal names its accepted set (`:87` "is not a detail level. Accepted: %s", `:105` "is not a format. Accepted: read") or its consequence (`:119` "is not a Blueprint, so it has no graphs to read", `:129` "has no graph named '%s'. Its graphs are: %s").

tasks.title: T-SUITE-01 (P3, medium) — The material suites DO assert the rollback text — but only on the paths the code verifies, which is why 28 unchecked sites are untested
tasks.description:
Summary
    A cross-layer result that reconciles two earlier ones. Ten suites were read, and the material suites do assert the exact rollback text from the C++ — but only on the paths the code itself verifies.

What the suites assert
    `test-material-tidy.py:53` asserts "FAILED: the layout changed the SET OF EXPRESSIONS, so it was ROLLED BACK." `test-material-label-promote.py:71` asserts "was ROLLED BACK." `test-material-blocks.py:72` asserts "FAILED: the edit LOST 1 expression(s) it did not list, so it was ROLLED BACK." All three also state that the fixture is restored on the way in and on the way out and that the restore is asserted (`:34`, `:43`, `:49`), and `test-material-label-promote.py:52` asserts the restore against what the suite did rather than against a count read from the asset — the verify-a-restore-against-the-set rule, already applied in the test layer.
    So the suites do test the rollback, and they assert the exact text the C++ prints.

Why the two earlier results coexist rather than contradict
    The suites assert the rollback on the paths the code verifies — "the set of expressions changed", "lost 1 expression it did not list" — and those paths compare something and report the comparison. The 28 unchecked cancels are on different paths: the ones that fire when `CreateMaterialExpressionEx` returns null, or when a usage node cannot be created. No suite makes an expression creation fail, so no suite exercises those paths.
    So the precise statement is narrower than "the rollback is untested": it is tested where the code measures, and untested where the code only assumes — and those are the twenty-eight sites.

The actionable form
    To close the class, a suite must make an expression creation fail and then assert that the transaction did not commit. `test-material-tidy.py` already has the machinery — `:374` mentions a run interrupted part-way that left the material mid-layout — so the fixture for the failure exists; what is missing is a case where the engine refuses the creation.

And it settles the question the suite rounds raised
    The test layer is not the problem. It tests what the code lets it test. The gap is that the code gives it nothing on twenty-eight paths, because on those paths the code does not check either.

tasks.title: T-C3-02 (P5, low) — C3 and C-P10 overlap on 16 sites: the C-P10 card owns them, and C3 owns only the comment question at those lines
tasks.description:
Summary
    The comment-versus-code card and the unchecked-write card overlap on sixteen sites. Thirteen of the remaining sites on the first card are already listed, with more detail, on the card about destructive operations with no checked result. This card exists so the work is not done twice.

The overlap, established by matching line numbers on both cards

    In `AcceptanceAssetCommandlet.cpp`: `:1138` (the asset file is deleted before the save, with no undo), `:1060` (a Blueprint renamed out of its package, the `Rename` bool discarded), and `:590`, `:596`, `:627`, `:708`, `:1014` (five links skipped silently).
    In `GraphTidy.cpp`: `:1306`, `:1382` (a link broken unconditionally, an undo not checked).

tasks.title: T-AUDIT-06 (P0, high) — AUDITED BY HAND 6/49: TurboMCPNodeId.cpp — 461 lines, a colon that breaks round-tripping, and a normaliser two of four callers skip
tasks.description:
Summary
    `TurboMCPNodeId.cpp` is the single place that turns a node ID into text and back, so every other tool depends on it. The 461 lines were read to the end and two problems came out.

What was found
    1. A colon in a graph name breaks the round trip. `Make` quotes a graph name containing a space (`:71-75`) and `Parse` strips those quotes (`:166-173`), but neither function does anything about a colon. A graph called `My:Graph` produces an ID that `Parse` reads back as graph `My` with node key `Graph` — a different graph, silently. Two comments disagree about it: `:161` says a colon "cannot be handled by an ID anyway", `:163` says the key "can always be found from the right". The code does neither.
    2. `FindNodesByKey` compares the key as given. It trims and lowercases only (`:219`) and then does a prefix test (`:232-233`), so a one-character key matches every node whose GUID starts with that character. `NormaliseKey` exists for exactly this and rejects a non-hex key (`:178-208`), but only two of its four callers use it (`CaptureSelector.cpp:759`, `:397`); `Capture.cpp:675` and `NodeResolve.cpp:343` pass the raw value.

What to do
    Quote a colon the same way a space is quoted, and delete whichever comment is wrong. Call `NormaliseKey` inside `FindNodesByKey`, and refuse a key shorter than `StandardKeyDigits` (6, `NodeId.h:33`) instead of padding it — padding to `300000` invents a GUID prefix and then reports "gone" when the truth is "four digits too few".

What is already right (do not re-investigate)
    `MakeKey` cannot emit a key shorter than the standard width (`:28-40`), which is why the prefix problem is reachable only through the reader. Lower-case GUID format is deliberate (`:28-30`). An unusable input yields an empty ID the caller must refuse on (`:46-51`). `UniqueKeyDigits` grows the prefix until unique and states that the loop is bounded (`:255-283`). `GetNodeTypeId` strips every whitespace character (`:404-406`), special-cases the custom-event form (`:427-433`) and returns an empty type ID for a node with no menu category (`:444-457`).

Note
    The file reads no asset and writes nothing, so a comment defect here costs nothing at runtime — except finding 1, which can resolve an ID to the wrong graph. Later audits found the same shape twice more: a `kind` no caller can ask for in `TurboMCPTypes.cpp`, and a `mutable` documented in `TurboMCPPanelToolRunner.h` that the code replaced with a `const_cast`.

tasks.title: T-AUDIT-11 (P1, medium) — AUDITED BY HAND 11/49: TurboMCPNodeResolve.cpp — 570 lines, a malformed key refused with a diagnosis about the graph, plus a continue where break is meant
tasks.description:
Summary
    `TurboMCPNodeResolve.cpp`, 570 lines. It is read-only — no transaction, no `Modify()`, no write of any kind — so the rollback family of defects cannot occur here. One finding, and it is the other side of the one found in `TurboMCPNodeId.cpp`.

What was found
    1. A malformed key is refused with a diagnosis about the graph instead of about the call. `:343` calls `FindNodesByKey` with `Parsed.NodeKey` and no `NormaliseKey` — the same omission as `Capture.cpp:675`. `NodeId.cpp:219` trims and lowercases only, so a key like `zz` produces zero matches and falls into the no-match branch at `:371-374`, which says "no node in %s:%s has the key %s. The node may have been deleted, or the graph rebuilt." A caller's mistake in the key therefore gets an answer about the graph. `zz` is not a deleted node, it is not a key — and the branch cannot tell the two apart, because both were reported as zero matches. The file states the standard it breaks at `:323-327`, where a wrong asset class is refused with its class named, because "saying which class it is prevents a second identical attempt".
       Fix: validate the key where it is parsed. `TurboMCPNodeId::NormaliseKey` is public (`NodeId.h:99`) and already refuses a non-hexadecimal key; refuse it there, naming the character that failed. That also closes the `FindNodesByKey` gap from the other side: a caller that cannot normalise is a caller that should not have to.
    2. `:355-358` uses `continue` where `break` is meant. `:351` sets `int32 Offered = 0`, then `:355` reads `if (Node == nullptr || Offered >= MaxNearMissTitles) { continue; }`. A `continue` on a cap test does not stop the loop — it skips that node and keeps iterating every remaining node, re-testing the cap each time. The answer stays correct because `Offered` stops growing, so this is a cost rather than a bug, but it is a full pass over a graph that has already been told to stop.

What is right (do not re-investigate)
    `:323-327` is the standard finding 1 breaks. `:347-369` is the opposite of a dead end: an ID whose node is gone says so and lists the nodes in that graph whose key is close, so a caller can find the survivor of a rebuild without guessing, and `:378-379` labels the list by its criterion so the reader does not have to infer it. `:385-392` refuses an ambiguous key rather than guessing — "handing back one of them would be a guess". `:336-337` refuses a missing graph with every graph name listed, so the answer contains the correction. `:76-78`: `InputIndex`, `OutputIndex` and `Shown` are all read, so this file has no dead counter, unlike the three material writers. `:240-241` carries both `ResolvedCount` and `RefusedCount`, so a partial resolution reports both halves rather than only the successes. `:494-500` carries `TotalMatched`, `Searched` and `HitsInGraph` — the denominator that `TurboMCPMaterialTidy.cpp` lacks.

Note
    The split found across the audit holds here too: files that write carry the rollback and counter defects, files that only read carry comment and refusal defects, and no file has shown both. This is the second time it appears.
