tasks.title: T-AUDIT-21-24 (P0, high) — AUDITED BY HAND 21-24/49: the tool-wrapper layer — one unguarded refusal prefix against a project rule that names the exact failure, and three pass-throughs that are correct
tasks.description:
Summary
    The tool-wrapper layer. `TurboMCPTraceTools.cpp` was read in full and the three wrappers that have no `Plan`/`Apply` were read as controls. One of those controls states the project's rule for exactly this problem, which settles the repair.

What was found
    One file prefixes a refusal without the guard the project uses everywhere else. `TurboMCPTrace.cpp:198` and `:221` fill `OutError` with a plain sentence and no prefix ("'%s' is not an action. This tool takes arm, clear or status."), while `:234` prefixes its own refusal in `Apply`. Then `TurboMCPTraceTools.cpp:39` wraps whatever comes back with `"error: %s"` unconditionally, and `:46` returns `Apply`'s result with nothing added. Because `Apply` already prefixes, the wrapper can print `error: error: ...`.
    The project has already written the rule down. `TurboMCPWidgetTreeTools.cpp` states it and implements it: the error prefix is added in exactly one place, with the same guard the material and block readers use, "because two layers each assuming the other leaves the prefix off is how a result ends up reading `error: error: ...`". Its test is on the result rather than on a flag, "because a flag can disagree with the string it describes".

What to do
    Test the result for the prefix before adding it. `:46` is already correct as it stands, because `Apply` owns its prefix — after the guard, both paths name their failure once.

The survey behind it
    36 `*Tools.cpp` files, all thin, with a regular shape: `Plan`, then `Apply` or `Render`. The four exceptions were read. `TurboMCPAssetCostTools.cpp` (25 lines) is one pass-through, and its header explains why the answer is split by provenance, quoting `D-52`: one total size was rejected because a total names no cause and cannot be acted on. `TurboMCPFunctionTools.cpp` (35 lines) is two pass-throughs, and its header explains why there is no preview twin — the name checks happen before anything is created, so a refusal changes nothing — and why the pair exists at all: remove is what frees a name that an add took by mistake. `TurboMCPWidgetTreeTools.cpp` (34 lines) is the guard above. `TurboMCPCallCostTools.cpp` is the outlier at 403 lines in a layer of 25-to-130-line wrappers.

Note
    The exposed set is the intersection of two things: a wrapper that does not guard, and an `Apply` that prefixes its own return. Seven implementations prefix it — `GraphKnots`, `LocalVars` (twice), `WidgetRetarget`, `Comment`, `MaterialBlocks`, `MaterialTidy`, `MaterialLabelsPromote` — while the four wrappers that do guard are all material wrappers calling `AsError`, an eleven-line helper with no dependencies in `TurboMCPMaterialTools.cpp`. Moving that helper and calling it from every wrapper makes the prefix appear exactly once whatever the implementations do.

tasks.title: T09 (P1, medium) — Add dedicated call-node swap with named-pin preservation
tasks.description:
Architectural decision
    Build a dedicated call-swap capability; do not overload `P/E-GRAPH-REPLACE`. GraphReplace rewrites an entire body and is destructive by design, while swapping one call is a localized transformation with distinct safety and reporting contracts. Reusing GraphReplace would make intent unclear, risk unrelated-node removal, and leave its unmatched-pin behavior undefined.

Public interface
    Add a Preview/Edit tool pair named `PreviewTurboMCPGraphSwapCall` and `EditTurboMCPGraphSwapCall` with:
    - `asset`: Blueprint in any accepted asset path form.
    - `graphName`: exact graph name.
    - `nodeId`: source call node ID as printed by `R-GRAPH-LOAD`.
    - `replacementTypeId`: canonical target call type ID, resolved through `FTurboMCPNodeType` in the same graph context.
    - `keepOld`: `true` means unlink and retain the original node; `false` means delete it after verified migration. Default must be `true` in the public tool metadata/documentation.

Required design
    1. Put parse/resolve/validation in a reusable plan class (for example `FTurboMCPGraphSwapCall`) so Preview and Edit share exactly one decision path.
    2. Refuse unless `nodeId` resolves to exactly one `UK2Node_CallFunction`; name the actual node class for a wrong node kind.
    3. Build the replacement through the existing action/type resolver, never by reconstructing engine function references manually.
    4. Map links by exact pin name and direction, never by pin index. For every source and destination link, record the old endpoint, proposed new endpoint, and verification result.
    5. A linked old pin absent from the replacement is a named refusal/report item; it must not be silently disconnected. The edit may proceed only for links that can be preserved safely, and its result must distinguish migrated, retained-unmatched, and refused links by pin name.
    6. Use one transaction. Before destructive unlinking, prove each proposed replacement link is allowed. On any failed migration or post-write verification, restore the original links and roll back using `FTurboMCPRollback`.
    7. With `keepOld=false`, remove the old node only after every preservable link is verified on the replacement; with `keepOld=true`, leave the old node present but unplugged and report its ID.
    8. Compile and independently read back the graph. The result must name the old node, new node, every migrated link, every unmatched pin, whether the old node was retained/deleted, and the comparison verdict.

Verification
    Create or use a focused fixture with a call that has at least four linked output pins and a replacement wrapper exposing the same output names in a different order. Assert each link is preserved by pin name, not index. Add a second case with an intentionally absent replacement pin and assert its name is reported and its original link is not silently dropped. Exercise both `keepOld=true` and `keepOld=false`; verify node/link state through `R-GRAPH-LOAD`, not the edit response.

Rationale
    This gives one narrow tool one narrow invariant: safely transform one call node. It avoids creating a second graph-text dialect, reuses the established asset/node/type/rollback primitives, and keeps whole-body replacement independent.

tasks.title: T10 (P1, medium) — Repoint every reader from one output to another
tasks.description:
Architectural decision
    Add a dedicated Preview/Edit graph-repoint capability. Do not overload GraphSwapCall: T09 transforms one call node, while T10 rewires all consumers of one output and may create the replacement source.

Public interface
    Add `PreviewTurboMCPGraphRepoint` and `EditTurboMCPGraphRepoint`:
    - `asset`, `graphName`: Blueprint and graph.
    - `sourceNodeId`, `sourcePin`: the output currently being read.
    - `targetNodeId`: existing source node ID; empty means create a new source node.
    - `targetTypeId`, `targetPin`: required only when creating a source; the canonical node type and output pin name.
    - `keepSource`: bool string, default true; the old source is never deleted by default.

Required design
    1. One side-effect-free plan is shared by Preview/Edit. Resolve the source exactly once and require an output pin. Resolve an existing target by exact node ID, or build a transient target probe with `FTurboMCPNodeType::BuildProbeNode` and list its actual output pins.
    2. Enumerate every linked consumer from the source output. Snapshot each consumer node ID, input pin name, and original endpoint. Do not mutate if no consumers exist.
    3. Existing target mode matches `targetPin` by exact name and direction. New-target mode uses the probe's exact pin and reports the created node's real ID/pin after apply. Refuse missing or direction-incompatible pins by name.
    4. Before breaking any source link, verify every proposed target connection with the schema. Apply one transaction; break and reconnect one link at a time; on any refusal or readback mismatch restore all original links and remove any created node through `FTurboMCPRollback`.
    5. Read back every consumer link independently. The result must list every repointed `consumerNodeId.consumerPin`, old source endpoint, new source endpoint, count, and whether the old source was retained. No silent subset success.
    6. Compile/mark structurally modified and distinguish `unchanged` refusal from `changed` result. `keepSource=false` may delete the old source only after all consumer links pass verification.

Verification
    Measure first with an existing multi-reader fixture. Then add a focused fixture/test for: existing target with multiple consumers; new target creation with reported node/pin; and a refused target pin proving the original links remain intact. Assert the set of repointed consumer pins from independent `R-GRAPH-LOAD` readback, not the edit response alone.

Rationale
    A dedicated rewire plan keeps the break-then-make rollback invariant visible, handles existing and newly-created sources as separate cases, and guarantees the answer names every moved reader.

tasks.title: T-FAST-1 (P0, high, TOP) — the fixture restore is what restarts the editor: make the restore cheap so one editor serves the whole run
tasks.description:
Summary
    The user reported this problem:
    "the current Test start stop engine is a flaw and slow down massively."
    The runner states the cause in a comment. The suites are not the cause.

The cause
    `Tools/run-suites.ps1:44-48` states this chain:
    "The restore below is what makes a full run green. The restore is also what stops the editor. `git checkout` answers `unable to unlink old ...: Invalid argument` while the editor holds the file open. So the harness must stop the editor first. A suite that saves an asset always makes the fixture dirty. A save-heavy run therefore restarts the editor again and again. That, not the suites, is where the minutes go."
    The chain in short. A suite saves an asset. The fixture becomes dirty. The harness must restore the fixture. `git checkout` cannot unlink a file that the editor holds open. The harness stops the editor and starts it again. The loop repeats for each suite that saves.

What `-Fast` fixes, and what it does not fix
    `-Fast` skips the between-suite restore. It restores once after the loop (`:433-441`). That step removes the restart. It does not remove the cause. The script buys the isolation back when it re-runs each failure alone.
    `:49-51` states the trade: "it is not the default, because a deferred restore lets a later suite see an earlier suite's fixture. That is exactly the `test-vcs` failure that the restore was added to fix."
    So `-Fast` is a mitigation, and it costs isolation. This card removes the cause instead. The editor then never stops, and you keep the speed and the isolation.

The work, in the order that pays
    1. Document the loop that exists today. No document mentions `-Fast`. A grep over README.md, DOCS.md, TOOLS.md and all of `Spec/` returns zero hits. `README.md:145-147` documents only the slow commands. Add one line: `run-suites.ps1 -Suites <name> -Fast` as the while-fixing command. That line makes the fast path the usual habit. It does not change the default behaviour.
    2. Remove the reason that the editor must stop. Measure three routes. Do not argue about them.
       - Restore the asset through the tools. That step runs in the process and does not unlink a file.
       - Restore the fixture before the editor opens the file. Then no process holds the file.
       - Copy over the file instead of unlinking it, if the engine accepts that operation where `git checkout` fails.
    3. Measure both audiences. Quote both numbers. Split each number into editor startup, test time and restore. The two audiences are a full sweep (production) and one suite against a running editor (the fix loop).

done when
    1. A full sweep and a single-suite run each have a measurement with the editor kept alive. The editor-startup share is a separate number from the test time.
    2. One suite runs against an already-running editor and pays no startup. "Edit, test, read the verdict" is then a loop, not a ceremony.
    3. Fixture isolation survives. The script names a suite that leaves the tree dirty, and the next suite's verdict is still its own. You prove this on the kept-alive path. You do not assume it.
    4. `-Fast`'s trade is gone, because the editor never stops, or the card documents the exact conditions for the switch.

Note
    This change risks fixture leakage. The project paid for that lesson once. `test-vcs` failed for exactly this reason before the per-suite restore existed. A kept-alive run that lets one suite's state reach the next one trades an hour for a green run that means nothing.
